name: Drometrizole trisiloxane
lead: Drometrizole trisiloxane (INCI name; sold by L'Oreal as Mexoryl XL, also called silatrizole) is a lipophilic, benzotriazole-derived organic ultraviolet filter used in sunscreens and daily-wear skincare products [1]. It is described as a broad-spectrum absorber with peaks near 303 nm (UVB) and 344 nm (UVA) and is frequently formulated together with ecamsule (Mexoryl SX) [1][2].

For appearance, its role is protective: by absorbing sunlight before it reaches the skin, sunscreens containing it limit the ultraviolet exposure that drives tanning, uneven pigmentation, sunburn and photoaging, so the skin keeps a clearer, more even tone over time [3][5]. Published work on the compound itself is mostly formulation, photoprotection and safety research rather than trials of cosmetic outcomes.
It is approved for sunscreens in the European Union, Canada, Australia, Japan and other countries but is not approved in the United States [1][11].

paras: The compound is a benzotriazole derivative bearing a siloxane group, with a molar mass of about 502 g/mol [1]. Reviews of sunscreen filters list it alongside terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid (Mexoryl SX) and methylene bis-benzotriazolyl tetramethylbutylphenol among the newer photostable filters [3].
Reviews of newer sunscreen filters discuss it among the photostable options, in contrast with older filters that lose absorbance more readily in sunlight [3].

It is used in sunscreen and daily skincare formulations to broaden UVA and UVB coverage [1][3]. Analytical chemistry papers include it among the UV filters monitored in commercial suncare products [4]. A study of sunscreens and skin pigmentation reported protection against UV-induced pigmentation by products containing Mexoryl filters [5].

Within formulations, it is typically paired with ecamsule (Mexoryl SX), a water-soluble UVA filter. In a study of protection against delayed pigmentation, the level of protection correlated with the concentration of Mexoryl SX, and the authors reported a synergistic effect when it was combined with Mexoryl XL [5].

Sunscreens containing Mexoryl filters have also been used in research on melanocytic nevi: in a small in vivo model of four nevi, a high-protection sunscreen containing octocrylene, Parsol 1789, titanium dioxide, Mexoryl SX and Mexoryl XL limited the melanocytic activation and pigmentation seen on unprotected halves of the lesions after UV exposure [12].

Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis to drometrizole trisiloxane in a sunscreen, with concomitant sensitivities to other sunscreen ingredients [6], and in a woman later diagnosed with frontal fibrosing alopecia [7]. A multicentre European photopatch study registered 1,000 participants to examine photocontact dermatitis from UV filters [8].

A toxicological risk assessment published in 2026 summarized animal and laboratory studies: oral and dermal LD50 values above 2 g/kg in rats, no skin or eye irritation in rabbits, no sensitization in guinea pigs, negative genotoxicity tests, no tumor formation in long-term dermal mouse studies, and no treatment-related reproductive or developmental effects at doses up to 1000 mg/kg/day [13]. The case reports of allergy described above are individual events in a product category that is widely used in Europe [6][7].

No clinical trial dedicated to drometrizole trisiloxane alone as a cosmetic ingredient has been published. Studies that included products containing it examined several outcomes using finished sunscreens, so effects cannot be attributed to this filter alone.

In a double-blind, intra-individual study, 11 patients with photosensitive lupus erythematosus were photoprovoked with UVA plus UVB; a sunscreen combining octocrylene, Mexoryl SX, Mexoryl XL, Parsol 1789 and titanium dioxide protected all 11 patients, while two other products protected fewer [9]. A pigmentation study measured protection against delayed UV pigmentation and reported higher prevention with the full Mexoryl formula, with a synergistic effect between the two Mexoryl filters [5]. A registered trial of UV and UV-visible light photoprotection in 68 melasma patients has been completed [10], and a multicentre European photopatch study registered 1,000 participants to examine photocontact dermatitis from UV filters [8]. Separately, a small study of patients with xeroderma pigmentosum who use stringent sun protection examined vitamin D levels [14].

Organic UV filters as a class have been measured in coastal waters, with a 2025 survey of 107 surface water samples from the East China Marginal Seas analyzing 22 organic filters including benzotriazole types [15]. Analytical methods have also screened for UV filters in food samples such as market tomatoes [16]. These studies describe presence and detection rather than effects on people.

It is permitted in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan, and is not approved in the United States [1]. A 2025 review argued that newer filters not available in the US could improve public health if regulations were modernized [11].

The 2025 review of US regulation describes drometrizole trisiloxane alongside bemotrizinol, bisoctrizole and terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid as filters used internationally that have not gained US approval, and points to the FDA's over-the-counter monograph order request process as a possible route [11]. Wikipedia lists EU, Canadian, Australian and Japanese approvals without giving a maximum concentration [1].

card.summary: Photostable L'Oreal UVA/UVB sunscreen filter (Mexoryl XL), approved in the EU and elsewhere but not in the US.
card.note: Not an FDA-approved US sunscreen active; rare contact-allergy case reports.

quick.overview:
Drometrizole trisiloxane, sold as Mexoryl XL, is an organic UV filter that absorbs both UVB and UVA light. It is commonly paired with ecamsule (Mexoryl SX) in sunscreens.

It is approved in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan but not in the United States. Evidence on it comes mainly from formulation and photoprotection studies of finished products.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs ultraviolet radiation, with peaks around 303 nm and 344 nm, and converts it to less harmful energy within the sunscreen film.
quick.risks: Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis to it. It is not an approved US sunscreen active, so US availability depends on products using other filters.

chain: Absorbs UVB and UVA light in the sunscreen film
Less UV-driven pigmentation, redness and photodamage
Clearer, more even-toned skin over the years
angle.text: Used as one active in a daily sunscreen, drometrizole trisiloxane widens the range of ultraviolet wavelengths the product absorbs. People who use such sunscreens do so to prevent tanning, dark spots and the visible signs of sun ageing. Studies of finished products containing it show reduced UV-induced pigmentation [5].
